extracted.intended_audience: novelists and serious fiction writers (and critics/students of narrative technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and using narrative point of view (first/third/epistolary) and on techniques for rendering a character's inner life as drama (showing vs telling, economy, authorial restraint). Emphasises when autobiography/first-person is appropriate or limiting and how to dramatize consciousness so the reader experiences the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of first-person narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal narrator 'will do very well and may be extremely helpful, so long as the story is only the reflection of life beyond and outside him'; but when 'the story begins to find its centre of gravity in his own life' the method is limited and may need to give way to a stronger one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person when the story's primary interest lies in describing an external world or events seen by the narrator. Avoid relying on first-person autobiography when the central material is the narrator's own inner life or when you need to dramatize complex thought processes; in such cases consider methods that put the consciousness itself before the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize consciousness rather than report it
rubrics_metrics.description: When the man in the book is expected to make a searching and elaborate portrait of himself, 'drama we want, always drama'—the consciousness ought to be dramatized rather than merely recounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render internal life as action: show the mind 'in the act of judging and reflecting' so the reader witnesses the agitation, impulses and reactions as they happen rather than only receiving retrospective reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the narrator stand between reader and mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the hero come between us and his active mind, do not let the heroine stand in front of her emotions and portray them—unless for cause, for some needful effect that would otherwise be missed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the emotional core of the book is the character's interiority, avoid modes that place an intermediary storyteller between reader and feeling; only retain such mediation for specific effects (e.g., irony, unreliable self-revelation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect (dramatic) methods to produce a straighter effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The more circuitous procedure on the part of the author produces a straighter effect for the reader; that is why, other things being equal, the more dramatic way is better than the less. It is indirect, as a method; but it places the thing itself in view, instead of recalling and reflecting and picturing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek ways to present events and thought indirectly—by showing scenes, behavior, and the immediate surface of thought—so the reader makes the inferences, rather than relying on direct authorial explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: match method intensity to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The method is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further. A story is damaged by too much treatment as by too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose how far into dramatization or psychological rendering to go based on what the subject requires. Over-dramatizing a story whose subject is communal or scenic (e.g., David Copperfield) can displace the centre and weaken the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epistolary/diary form to dramatize contemporaneous emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a story out of a series of letters or a running diary is 'engaged in the attempt to show a mind in action' and keeps emotion 'in the foreground' by making it contemporaneous rather than retrospective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letters/diary to capture immediacy and recurring suspense (Clarissa's daily agonies are an example). Be aware of practical drawbacks: contrivances to preserve verisimilitude, forced distances between characters, and the strain of maintaining plausibility over long stretches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render thought via its surface movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist 'represents it by means of the movement that flickers over the surface of his mind. The impulses and reactions of his mood are the players upon the new scene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing a mind, show the passing images, impulses, looks, tones and small reactions that manifest thought. Let these surface phenomena do the narrative work, as theatrical action would for a stage character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial restraint—do not supply hidden knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Henry James 'knows all there is to know of Strether, but he most carefully refrains from using his knowledge.' The author must avoid entering to explain the inner substance of the mind he is dramatizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from authorial exposition about characters' private thoughts; present only what can be observed in the mind's surface and let the reader infer deeper meaning. If the author begins to expound, the reader will assume full disclosure and the artful suspense will be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective narration when immediacy is required
rubrics_metrics.description: A retrospect in the words of the young man could not have given Raskolnikov 'thus bodily into the reader’s possession'—retrospective account lacks the conviction of immediate, enacted mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is to immerse the reader in the immediacy of inner experience (as in Crime and Punishment), prefer methods that present thought and feeling as they occur rather than as remembered and summarized later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader inhabit the character's experience
rubrics_metrics.description: By dramatizing a mind 'any one who has been through the book has truly become Raskolnikov, and knows exactly what it was to be that young man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for techniques (e.g., interior dramatization, close focalization) that allow readers to feel and think with the character so the experience is shared rather than merely reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: If the subject is a character's inner change, tell through that consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject of the book is Strether’s change of mind, 'the subject can only be reached through Strether’s consciousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a point of view that makes available the perceptual material and gradations of thought that constitute the subject. If the moral or thematic centre is the inner change, the narrative perspective must grant access to that inner process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve dramatic suspense by withholding full penetration
rubrics_metrics.description: When Strether’s mind is dramatized, 'nothing is shown but the passing images that anybody might detect' and 'below the surface, behind the outer aspect of his mind, we do not penetrate; this is drama, and in drama the spectator must judge by appearances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the mind to reveal itself gradually through surface appearances and successive moments; do not attempt to penetrate to a complete interior explanation, because drama gains power from measured revelation and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance picture-making freedom with dramatic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: By dramatizing a mind 'he forfeits none of his special freedom... the man’s mind has become visible, phenomenal, dramatic; but in acting its part it still lends us eyes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors need not sacrifice panoramic or descriptive freedom when dramatizing thought; you can retain wide-ranging picture-making even while making the mind visible—use the character's perception to extend vision rather than rely on authorial summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of contrivances required by a chosen method
rubrics_metrics.description: Richardson's epistolary novels 'are forced to pay heavily' with 'desperate shifts' to maintain verisimilitude (keeping friends at a distance, relayed reports, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a form (epistolary, strict first-person recollection, etc.), anticipate logistical and plausibility costs and weigh whether the dramatic gain justifies these narrative contortions.
